text: Authorization tells you whether testing a client is allowed at all. Scope is the practical work of turning that authorization into a precise map — exactly which systems, applications, and techniques are in bounds, so neither side is ever surprised by what actually gets touched once testing starts.

Real scoping documents name systems explicitly rather than describing them loosely. The in-scope web app and API range are listed by exact hostname and IP block, while payroll systems, production payment processing, and physical offices are explicitly excluded. Notice the last line of a good scope: anything not named is out of bounds by default. That protects the tester from disputes over systems nobody ever agreed to test.

A handful of categories cause more scope disputes than anything else, so professional scoping addresses them every time. Does authorization reach the client's underlying cloud infrastructure, or only the application layer — remember, AWS and Azure both publish their own acceptable-use policies for security testing. Is denial-of-service testing in scope at all, given it's almost always excluded from production. Is social engineering of named employees or physical premises included, which needs its own sign-off. And how is any sensitive data accessed during testing handled and destroyed afterward.

This happens constantly: a scan of an in-scope subnet turns up a reachable server that was never named in the scope document. The professional answer is never to test it anyway because it seems basically in scope — that's exactly the unauthorized-access problem from Lesson 1. Instead, document what was observed from outside it, and go back to the client for a written scope amendment. Scope changes mid-engagement are completely normal; testing without that amendment is not.

That's how scope turns a signed authorization into something both sides can actually point to and agree on. Next lesson, we look at what happens once scope is locked down — the real, published methodology a professional engagement follows from first contact to final report, grounded in the Penetration Testing Execution Standard and the OWASP Testing Guide.
